SDS 336 · Midterm project checkpoint
Which Austin crimes get solved, and why?
Five data-backed hypotheses from 2.68 million Austin Police Department crime reports, 2003–2026
Palash Pawar · Karthikaya Kasa · Varun Bandaru · Sai Koduri · Vinay Devarakonda · Saisarath Bolneni
October 2026
The data
Every APD crime report since 2003
2.68M
incidents, one row each
23 yrs
Jan 2003 to Oct 2026
450
offense types (top 20 = 69%)
Three data quirks shaped everything that follows
Clearance coding changed in 2009
Before 2009, 60% of statuses are missing. We use 2009+ for all clearance analysis.
26% of times end in :00
Exact-minute times would give about 1.7%. This anomaly became H2.
"Cleared" = solved
Cleared by arrest or by exception. Overall, 27.5% of 2009–2025 cases are cleared.
Source: City of Austin Open Data Portal, "Crime Reports" (downloaded Oct 12, 2026) · 2
H1 · Logistic regression
Fast reports get solved; late ones rarely do
0.42
odds ratio for clearance per 10× longer delay, same offense
Hypothesis
For property and street crimes, a late report lowers the chance of clearance beyond crime type. Murder and rape don't depend on delay.
SDS 336 · Austin crime reports · 3
H2 · Timestamp anomaly + logistic regression
26% of times are rounded to the hour, and those cases are cleared less often
0.61
odds ratio for a rounded time, with offense and delay held fixed
Hypothesis
A rounded time records that nobody saw the crime. Such cases are cleared less often, even at the same offense and delay.
SDS 336 · Austin crime reports · 4
H3 · Direct standardization
Clearance fell from 34% to 17% after 2017
59%
of the 2009→2021 drop remains with the 2009–12 crime mix held fixed
Hypothesis
The same kinds of cases are cleared less often. The sharp 2018 break points to an institutional change (staffing, policy or reporting).
SDS 336 · Austin crime reports · 5
Tested, not supported
We expected family violence to spike during the 2020 lockdown. It didn't.
+2.2%
Mar–Aug 2020 vs the 2015–19 trend + seasonality baseline. Normal noise is ±5%.
The family-violence share did rise in 2020, but mostly because it had been trending up since 2015. Looking at daily data instead led us to the holiday pattern in H4.
SDS 336 · Austin crime reports · 6
H4 · Linear regression on daily counts
Family violence rises on holidays while other crime falls
+38%
family violence on Christmas Day, while all other incidents fall 29%
Hypothesis
Family-violence risk follows time families spend together, not overall activity in the city.

Next steps
Final project: predict which cases get cleared
01
Features from our hypotheses
  • Report delay (H1)
  • Rounded-time flag (H2)
  • Neighborhood profile / PC1 (H5)
  • Offense, family-violence flag, time of day
02
Models and validation
  • Logistic regression baseline
  • Then trees and ensembles (random forest, boosting)
  • Train 2009–2019, test 2022–2025, since H3 shows the pattern shifts over time
03
Feedback we'd like
  • What else could explain the 2018 break in clearance?
  • Is a rounded time a fair proxy for "nobody saw it"?
